No, Everything Does Not Happen for a Reason

“And we know that in all things God works for the good of those who love Him, who have been called according to His purpose” (Romans 8:28).

This isn’t a heavenly insurance policy paid with faith and exempting us from anything unpleasant, but the promise that if we choose to respond to all things from a place of love and goodness; that we—not necessarily our circumstances—will be better for it.

Bad exegesis in service to a flawed thesis.

We don't have to figure out the purpose for our pain, but we do follow a God who meets us in it.

Not knowing the purpose and rejecting the existence of a purpose are two completely different things. Ephesians 1:11 makes it clear that God is indeed sovereign over everything and works things according to his will.

Romans 8:28, is not, as TFA would twist it, some call be the change or a command to be good and good things will happen. It is a promise of God that, even when things suck worse than you ever thought possible, He is trustworthy and good and your suffering isn't pointless.

God hath decreed in Himself, from all eternity, by the most wise and holy counsel of His own will, freely and unchangeably, all things, whatsoever comes to pass;
So, in your understanding, do things happen that aren't according to God's will?

I affirm the confession where it states:

God hath decreed in himself, from all eternity, by the most wise and holy counsel of his own will, freely and unchangeably, all things, whatsoever comes to pass; yet so as thereby is God neither the author of sin nor hath fellowship with any therein; nor is violence offered to the will of the creature, nor yet is the liberty or contingency of second causes taken away, but rather established; in which appears his wisdom in disposing all things, and power and faithfulness in accomplishing his decree. (1689 LBCF 3:1)

Thus, nothing in all the universe happens except what is in accord with God's decretive will.
So God wanted the shooter to kill the Christians in that church in Charleston? Is that what following this logic concludes?

It was a sin for Joseph's brothers to sell him into slavery, but God meant for it to happen (Genesis 50:20). It was a grievous sin for the Jews and Romans to murder Jesus, but God meant for it to happen (Isaiah 53:10, Acts 2:23). It was a sin for the Huaorani people to murder Jim Elliot, but God meant for it to happen. In all these things, we can now know, at least in part, the good reasons why God meant them to happen.

Even in something like what happened in Charleston, where we have no idea why God meant them to happen, the promise of God is no less true. He works all things together for good, whether or not He lets us know that good end in this life.

The choices we have when thinking about what happened in Charleston are:

  1. God didn't know what would happen.
  2. God knew what would happen, but couldn't stop it.
  3. God knew what would happen, but just didn't stop it.
  4. God knew what would happen, and meant for it to happen.

The first denies the foreknowledge of God. The second denies the power of God. The third denies the goodness of God. The fourth affirms the promises of God.

I would go with #3 because I think #4 denies the goodness of God more. #3 could be explained by His desire to have free will creatures. That desire and the benefits that come from that desire are an example of His goodness. The benefits of free will outweigh the negatives of being automatons.

So I would say that it happened because we live in a fallen world chosen by our own free will. A person decided to do evil as a choice of his own free will. God didn't intervene because He didn't want to violate free will in this case. And God will now use this to bring glory to Himself.

The issue is still that God does intervene at times and not at others. Even in viewing it as #3, I have to wonder why God didn't intervene. Even being an open theist doesn't give God an out here because God knew when Dylan Roof would commit the crime, yet God didn't stop him then. That's where my explanation has to steer into #4 a little.

In #4, God completely chooses to have people be fatherless and motherless to make a point. God chose to ruin the criminal's life to make a point. And He used all this suffering to make a point that He could have made in a different way because we don't have free will.

But I would still argue that #4 denies the goodness of God much more than #3.

The benefits of free will outweigh the negatives of being automatons.

You mean this as an argument for (3), but I think it's really a disguised argument for (4). You're effectively giving human free will as the reason why God meant for the evil to happen. To support choice (3), you have to affirm that God knows exactly what bad things will occur, and He lets them happen for no reason. Instead, you argue that God knows exactly what bad things will occur, and He lets them happen for the reason "to have free will creatures". "God chooses to have people be fatherless and motherless to make a point" that it is more important "to have free will creatures".

The difference between you and me, then, would be that I don't explicitly claim to know the reason God meant it to happen.
God doesn't mean for evil to happen. He allowed for the possibility of evil. He hopes that humans will use it for good rather than evil.

"God doesn't mean for evil to happen", but Genesis 50:20 and Isaiah 53:10 mean this can't be true in every case.

"He allowed for the possibility of evil.", but Revelation 13:8 calls Christ "the Lamb slain from the foundation of the world" meaning evil was not a possibility but a certainty.

"He hopes", but "hope that is seen is not hope. For who hopes for what he sees?" Is hope a possibility for the God who knows?

I am an open theist, so I don't believe the future has happened yet. I also think that when God plans something, He will make it happen in His sovereignty. So when he planned for the Lamb to be slain at the foundation of the world, he knew He would do that.

Here is a post on why God does not know the future: http://regansravings.blogspot.com/2011/01/god-does-not-know-future.html
